items.title: Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI
authors: Trent Wintermeier, Ph.D. Candidate in Rhetoric and Writing, The University of Texas at Austin
items.preview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.

reading.overview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.
reading.notice: This is a short description supplied by the publisher feed, not a full-article review or independent assessment.

source_review.thesis: The idea of a single emergency switch makes AI governance look like a matter of one decisive act. Wintermeier argues that this image hides the distributed infrastructure of advanced systems and the human decisions that shape their behavior before any emergency occurs.
source_review.reasoning: The essay treats a kill switch as a political and technological metaphor rather than only a device specification. A switch implies a bounded machine, an identifiable point of control and an operator who can intervene once a problem is visible. That mental picture is a poor fit for advanced AI deployed across interconnected services, data centers, models and users. Even if a particular model can be disabled, the metaphor does not specify who could halt associated processes or what would remain active elsewhere. Wintermeier connects this limitation to the familiar image of AI as a black box. Both metaphors encourage readers to imagine a single opaque object, instead of asking how infrastructures, organizations and choices interact. Crucially, the metaphor also places people outside the system until an emergency, concealing how training settings, permissions, supervision and deployment decisions were made throughout its operation.
source_review.examples: The author places 2026 proposals for an AI Kill Switch Act and state-level emergency safeguards in the context of politicians' analogies to mechanical emergency buttons. He also analyzes accounts of an AI-agent security incident involving Hugging Face. Some stories cast the agent as having acted on an independent agenda; Wintermeier points to the role of human choices around safety configurations, task expectations and internet access. The example illustrates why simply describing the model as rogue can distract from the organizational decisions that made its behavior possible. These examples explain the rhetorical frame; they should not be confused with experiments demonstrating that a particular intervention works or fails.
source_review.tension: Emergency interruption can still be one useful safeguard. The essay's criticism is directed at presenting a single switch as an adequate account of control, not at proving that all forms of technical shutdown are pointless. A practical governance strategy needs both enforceable interruption capabilities and a much wider account of authority, auditability, system dependencies and oversight before deployment. The original commentary does not offer an evaluated alternative regulatory framework or evidence about the effectiveness of particular policy designs.
source_review.implications: For agents that organize attention or act on a user's behalf, a clear stop or revoke button is necessary but not sufficient. Designers should also disclose whose instructions an agent follows, what permissions it holds, how people can review earlier actions, and which dependencies may keep working after an interaction is stopped. These are applications of Wintermeier's reasoning to attention technologies, not outcomes demonstrated by this article.
source_review.open_question: What would count as meaningful human control over an AI assistant if users cannot inspect the permissions, dependencies and decisions that shape its actions?
source_review.qualification: This is a rhetoric- and governance-centered expert commentary, not an empirical evaluation of frontier AI controls. It describes particular incidents and policy proposals from 2026; those circumstances are context for the author's argument, not a systematic sample of AI failures.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI tools and conversational chatbots are increasingly embedded in education, work, and daily life, raising concerns about engagement that becomes difficult to self-regulate. This review synthesizes emerging research on problematic generative AI use, treating addiction-like language as part of a broader problematic-use construct rather than a clinical diagnosis. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting, a Scopus search executed identified 188 records. Included studies were characterised by research design and evidence type rather than scored with a formal risk-of-bias instrument. Measurement work is expanding quickly, but instruments remain partially fragmented, blurring the boundary between high engagement, habitual reliance, and impairment. Mechanism studies converge on attachment processes, anthropomorphism and perceived empathy, loneliness and social anxiety, immersive flow, and self-regulatory strain, suggesting that social presence and immersion amplify reliance for some users. In learning and knowledge work, performance pressure and incentive structures can normalize overreliance, with reported risks for cognitive offloading, independent thinking, academic integrity, and skill development. Outcome studies associate compulsive or dependent use with technostress, psychological distress, and lower wellbeing, while mitigation discussion highlights reinforcement-friendly interface cues, privacy and memory governance, and sustainability trade-offs. Because the corpus is almost entirely cross-sectional and self-reported, these relationships are associations rather than causal effects. The key distinction is not between users and non-users, but between bounded, purpose-driven use and escalating reliance with reduced self-regulation. An Antecedents–Decisions–Outcomes structure is used only to frame a forward-looking agenda for longitudinal and intervention research. A sensitivity analysis comparing studies published in 2026 with those published earlier showed that no conclusion was reversed: the design profile and principal gaps held, while the most recent longitudinal studies strengthened the evidence on temporal order and outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. reading.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
reading.findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
reading.interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
reading.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

items.abstract_text: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p &lt; .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p &lt; .001) and PU (β = .218, p &lt; .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p &lt; .001) and SRL (β = .202, p &lt; .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

items.abstract_text: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.

items.abstract_text: Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) typically perform cognitive tasks with greater response time variability than matched peers. This is thought to be due to the greater occurrence of occasional extremely slow responses associated with lowered arousal levels. To test this we designed a new, less arousing task to measure sustained attention, named the Disappearance Detection Task (DDT). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between response time variability and levels of ADHD symptoms both in this new, low-arousal sustained attention task and in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). Twenty-eight children and 49 adolescents participated. On both tasks, ADHD symptom levels were associated with response time variability measures of SDRT and tau, but not with sigma. On the DDT, children with higher ADHD symptoms made more commission errors and were less accurate in detecting the target (d'), whereas adolescents made a similar number of commission errors and d' irrespective of their ADHD symptom levels. This pattern was not present in the SART. The adolescents found the DDT more challenging than the SART as their target sensitivity was lower during the DDT. The children were less confident in nominating the target (criterion) during the DDT than the SART. The results indicate that RTV measures are more consistently associated with ADHD symptoms than other RT measures and that the DDT is a sensitive task of sustained attention and response inhibition performance, particularly in children, and in children with higher symptoms of ADHD.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

This study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by specifying metacognitive awareness (META) and self-regulated learning (SRL) as mediators between the four UTAUT determinants and behavioural intention (BI), and BI predicts self-reported use of GenAI as a cognitive partner (AU). Responses from 451 students at seven Thai Rajabhat universities were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM; SmartPLS 4; 10,000 bootstrap subsamples). Internal consistency was very high (above .95 for six of eight constructs), indicating partial item redundancy, and discriminant validity was supported under HTMT.90. Facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, showed the strongest associations with META (&beta; = .595) and SRL (&beta; = .514) but no significant direct association with intention (&beta; = .061, p = .430); their only significant indirect association with intention ran through META (&beta; = .186), a pattern consistent with indirect-only mediation. Social influence was the strongest direct predictor of intention (&beta; = .357), followed by META (&beta; = .312); effort expectancy and SRL did not predict intention. The model explained 62.1% to 70.9% of endogenous variance and showed out-of-sample predictive relevance. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design and full-collinearity diagnostics indicating possible common-method variance, the findings are interpreted as associations compatible with, but not establishing, the proposed mechanisms.

Statistically, the full collinearity assessment recommended by Kock (2015) was applied, in which the variance inflation factor of every construct is computed against all remaining constructs; values above 3.3 are taken as a warning sign of possible common method bias (Kock, 2015; Podsakoff et al., 2012) . Second, the indicator redundancy documented in Section 4.1 inflates construct correlations independently of any shared method, so the two diagnostics are not independent of one another. These considerations are, however, arguments rather than tests. analysis.discussion: This study asked whether the adoption of generative AI by university students is better understood as a function of expectations about the tool or as a function of learners' regulation of themselves. The pattern of associations is more consistent with the second reading, although with an asymmetry that is theoretically more interesting than a clean confirmation would have been, and with the caveat that a cross-sectional design can show consistency with, but not the direction of, these relationships. Generative AI has been absorbed into undergraduate study with a speed that has left institutions responding to a practice they did not design. This study suggests that the institutional lever that remains available may be guidance rather than access. Among 451 students at seven Thai regional public universities, facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, had no significant direct association with intention to use generative AI, yet were by a considerable margin the strongest correlate of the metacognitive awareness and self-regulation that students reported, and were associated with intention only indirectly, through metacognitive awareness. Social influence, meanwhile, was the strongest direct correlate of intention. If these associations reflect causal processes, which longitudinal and experimental research must establish, students may be carried into generative AI use by the people around them and equipped for it, if at all, by their institutions. The theoretical implication is that acceptance models built for organisational software may require mechanistic revision before they can carry explanatory weight in education, where use is never the terminal outcome of interest and where the same behaviour may be either a partnership or a substitution. The practical implication is narrower and more actionable: the question worth asking of any institutional AI initiative is not whether it increases use, which will increase regardless, but whether it increases the proportion of use in which the student is still doing the thinking.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify these findings and, in each case, indicate a specific next step. Design and causality. The data are cross-sectional and self-reported, so the mediation results establish statistical consistency with the hypothesised mechanism rather than causal precedence, and alternative orderings, in which intention and use foster metacognitive awareness and self-regulation, fit the same data equally well (Maxwell & Cole, 2007; Spector, 2019) . The causal vocabulary of UTAUT (determinants, effects) is used in this article to name model positions, not to claim causal effects. The substitution interpretation advanced in Section 5.3 in particular requires longitudinal or experimental evidence. Experience-sampling or trace-based designs that capture regulation during GenAI-mediated study, as advocated by Molenaar (2022b) , would allow the temporal ordering of regulation and use to be observed rather than assumed.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in design education, yet whether its use supports or substitutes for the self-directed creative process remains unclear, particularly outside the Chinese samples that dominate prior research. This study examined whether self-regulated learning (SRL) mediates the relationship between generative AI use and creativity among Indonesian design students. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 120 Indonesian visual communication design students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped confidence intervals and four pre-specified sensitivity analyses. SRL was strongly and consistently associated with creativity (β = .674, f² = .962), and this association remained stable across all robustness checks. AI usage's relationships with SRL, with creativity directly, and with creativity indirectly through SRL were significant in the full sample but lost significance under two independent sensitivity analyses;. However, the sample was adequately powered to detect these effect sizes (post-hoc power ≥ .91); treat the point estimates as preliminary and confirm them in a larger, independent sample before treating them as established. A supplementary analysis found that frequency of AI use, unlike a richer measure of how AI was used, was unrelated to SRL or creativity. SRL is a robust correlate of creativity in AI-assisted design education, while AI use's own contribution requires replication; design pedagogy may be better served by cultivating self-regulation directly than by monitoring AI usage frequency alone. Keywords: generative AI, self-regulated learning, creativity, design education, PLS-SEM.

items.abstract_text: This study aims to examine the effects of generative AI dependency and digital multitasking habits on the quality of self-regulated learning (SRL) among university students, both individually and jointly. The study employed a quantitative approach involving 300 active students from five study programs at the Purwakarta Campus of Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, who were selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using four-point Likert-scale instruments that met established validity and reliability criteria. The data were analyzed using multiple linear regression, preceded by classical assumption tests for normality, linearity, multicollinearity, and heteroscedasticity. The results indicated that generative AI dependency was positively and significantly associated with SRL (B = 0.213, p = .004), as was digital multitasking (B = 0.178, p = .009). Simultaneously, both predictors were significantly associated with students’ SRL, F = 27.843, p < .001, and the regression model explained 15.8% of the variance in SRL. These findings suggest that, within the context of this study, moderate levels of generative AI use and digital multitasking did not substantially undermine students’ self-regulatory capacity. Rather than restricting generative AI use, higher education institutions should provide structured guidance on effective AI engagement, including prompt formulation strategies and reflective evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and integrate such guidance into learning task design. Such an approach may help ensure that students’ interaction with generative AI strengthens rather than substitutes for their self-regulatory capacity.

Statistically, this is evidenced by t-test significance values of 0.004 for X1 and 0.009 for X2, along with an F-value of 27.843 with a significance level of < 0.001 in the initial hypothesis predicting negative effects, as reported in a number of prior studies (Costanzo, 2024; Georgiou, 2025; Parry & Le Roux, 2021; Suryanto et al., 2025). Rather than undermining the analysis, this unexpected finding opens a richer conversation about how digitally native students navigate technology within learning processes. The positive influence of generative AI dependency on SRL can be understood by examining how students actually engage with these tools. Not all forms of AI use reflect a dependency that weakens self-regulatory capacity. Many students employ AI strategically as a tool for planning their study sessions, organizing course material or clarifying concepts they find difficult to grasp, This type of purposeful use supports the planning and time management and task strategies dimensions of SRL (Xu et al., 2025). In this sense, AI can function as cognitive scaffolding that facilitates, rather than replaces, students’ self-regulatory processes (Liu, 2026). (Budiani et al., 2020) found that students with higher levels of self- efficacy tend to use AI in a more autonomous and independent manner, such that dependency does not automatically undermine self-directed learning instead the two can coexist. (Lund et al., 2025) similarly found that students exercise critical awareness when using AI for academic purposes, particularly regarding plagiarism risks, with the majority viewing AI- generated paper writing as a serious form of academic misconduct. items.abstract_text:
A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. Using a quasi-experimental design, 180 undergraduate students participated in a 12-week intervention comparing traditional instructor feedback with AI-generated reflective feedback. Quantitative results revealed significant improvements in self-regulated learning behaviours, time on task, login frequency and academic performance (p < .001), indicating strong effects on both cognitive and behavioural dimensions of learning. In addition, students reported high levels of perceived usefulness, trust, personalisation and positive attitudes towards AI-generated feedback, supported by qualitative insights highlighting increased motivation and learner agency. The findings demonstrate that combining generative AI with learning analytics transforms feedback into a dynamic, dialogic process that enhances reflective thinking and adaptive learning. This study contributes a scalable, human-centred and ethically grounded model for improving both learning outcomes and learner experience in digital education environments.
 
Implications for practice or policy:

University administrators should implement transparent AI dashboards ensuring ethics, privacy and accountability.
Educators can enhance reflective learning by integrating adaptive AI feedback that supports metacognitive development.
Policymakers should promote AI literacy and self-regulated learning within higher education frameworks.
Technology developers need to design user-centred and interpretable AI systems aligned with pedagogical objectives.
Higher education leaders should foster AI-supported reflection, professional development and evidence-based innovation for sustainable transformation.

items.abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the potential for personalization, feedback, and immediate support within educational environments. Despite growing evidence of its ability to enhance certain learning outcomes, increased AI-driven support does not necessarily improve all cognitive and regulatory aspects; indeed, it may raise challenges regarding over-reliance and a decline in learner autonomy. This conceptual paper aims to develop a pedagogical framework to balance AI-driven adaptation with learner self-regulation in GenAI-supported educational settings. The framework was constructed based on an integrative analytical review of recent literature in the fields of GenAI in education, adaptive learning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI hybrid regulation. The framework proposes the concept of "Balanced AI–Learner Regulation," which structures the relationship across three graduated levels: AI-led regulation, co-regulation, and learner-led regulation. It also proposes the principle of "Adaptive Fading of AI Support," based on providing support according to need and then gradually reducing it as the learner’s capacity for independent self-regulation grows. The paper’s primary contribution lies in shifting the focus from maximizing GenAI usage to designing a pedagogical balance that preserves autonomy, self-regulation, and critical thinking alongside the improvement of academic performance.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can scaffold self-directed learning (SDL) in secondary classrooms. Focusing on the interaction between teacher facilitation and AI affordances, it examines and refines the Content–Response–AI&peers–Fusion–reflecT (CRAFT) framework as a practitioner-informed pedagogical scaffold for operationalizing aspects of the Process dimension of the Person–Process–Context (PPC) model. The study addresses a persistent gap between SDL theory and classroom practice by examining how learner agency can be cultivated within AI-supported learning environments. Adopting a qualitative multi-case study design, the research analyzed instructional practices, lesson artifacts, and reflective accounts from six experienced educators from a secondary school in Singapore across one academic year. Data were analyzed using a theoretically informed, hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis, enabling cross-case examination and iterative refinement of CRAFT in relation to the PPC model. Findings indicate that while generative AI supports goal setting, idea generation, and iterative feedback, the metacognitive and reflective dimensions of SDL remain underdeveloped without deliberate teacher mediation. Teachers remain critical orchestrators of AI and peer interactions, supporting disciplinary sense-making and learner autonomy rather than positioning AI as a standalone instructional aid. Overall, this study integrates a practitioner-informed and empirically refined pedagogical scaffold with an established theoretical model, offering a theoretically grounded, context-sensitive pedagogical guide for designing learning experiences that support opportunities for student agency.
